description: E1c's SECOND discriminator, and the one the first left open. osc_naive_sine (undriven pitch) and osc_naive_pitched (pitch pinned to 5 V) both measure -73.5 dBFS cross-platform, which killed the 'undriven input' hypothesis -- but voice_midi_note uses the SAME SE Oscillator (naive) and measures -123.1. The only remaining difference between them is the PITCH VALUE: 440.0 Hz against MIDI note 64. This case is the naive oscillator at note 64's value and nothing else changed, so it separates 'the residual depends on the specific phase increment' from 'something in the voice chain does the work'. 4.583333 V = 5 V minus 5 semitones, on the 1 V/octave convention where 5 V is 440 Hz (note 69).
tolerance_reason: Measured on Linux x86_64 (Ubuntu 24.04, glibc 2.39) against this case's reference, SynthEditCL V1.6.192, 2026-08-23 (E1c): null -140.1 dBFS, peakdiff -90.3 dBFS = 1 LSB at 16 bits. THE PRE-COMMITTED OUTCOME WAS THE ROUNDING BRANCH AND THIS IS IT, with 17 dB to spare against the -123 the case named. So the provisional drift-class gates this case shipped with are RETIRED and it now runs at the project defaults (-100/-86), which are the rounding-class budget. What this decides, per the case's own pre-commitment: the discriminator is the PITCH VALUE, not the module and not whether the pitch input is driven. Refined by the same run, because the binary was too coarse: the naive oscillator at note 64 is rounding class (-140.1) while at 440.0 Hz it is drift class (-73.5, E1a), AND the core Oscillator at 440.0 Hz is rounding class (-131.1, same run) -- so neither the module nor the pitch alone is the variable. It is the naive oscillator AT 440.0 Hz specifically.
